opportunities.title: Two-office intake, triage and document-chase agent that owns the Jan–Apr front door
opportunities.problem: Every inbound client contact across both offices funnels into one phone number (732-257-8604) and one generic inbox (info@matthewsandnulty.com), with no online booking: the homepage's 'Schedule Consultation' button just re-opens the WPForms contact page. Callers are therefore not routed by location or service, nothing is triaged after hours, and the firm publishes no hours or after-hours channel at all. In a firm whose service mix (individual tax, business tax, payroll, HOA accounting) all peaks on the same federal deadlines, intake is handled manually by whoever is at the desk.
evidence: Both offices — East Brunswick and the Hazlet office added in late 2023 — list the same phone number and the same single email; there is no per-office line or inbox (https://matthewsandnulty.com/contact)

New-client intake is a WPForms form (name, email, phone, service dropdown, message) behind a math captcha, and the 'Schedule Consultation' call-to-action links only to that contact page; no booking calendar exists anywhere on the site (https://matthewsandnulty.com/contact)

The firm's own site publishes no business hours, after-hours number or emergency contact; a Mon–Fri 9AM–5PM, closed-weekend schedule appears only on a third-party directory (https://www.loc8nearme.com/new-jersey/east-brunswick/matthews-and-nulty-inc/6592928/)

O*NET work context for tax preparers records structural seasonality — 55% report seasonal work schedules and 38% face time pressure every day — which concentrates exactly this intake load into one quarter (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/13-2082.00)

Clients already work in a self-service document channel: the site's main navigation links a hosted client portal, and a reviewer singles the portal out as useful, so documents and account context exist to be read by an agent (https://matthewsandnulty.com/)
opportunities.agent_design: An intake agent sits on the shared inbox and the web form: it reads each message (and call-transcript/voicemail drops if the phone system can export them), classifies it by office, service line and urgency, answers routine questions from the firm's own service pages and calendar, and either books the appointment or proposes slots. It then runs the document chase — a per-engagement checklist (IDs, prior-year return, P&L, bank statements) that it requests, tracks, and re-requests from the portal or email until complete, and it pushes everything into a single queue tagged East Brunswick or Hazlet. Triggers: new form submission, new email to the shared inbox, a document arriving in the portal, and a 48-hour no-response timer. It hands off cleanly: a staff member or partner sees one prioritised list each morning instead of an inbox, and approves every appointment that falls outside published hours, every new-client engagement, and every message it could not classify (it drafts a reply and stops). Everything that touches return data stays inside a vetted/private deployment because of IRC Sec. 7216 limits on disclosing return information and the FTC Safeguards Rule's service-provider oversight duty for tax preparers (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/7216).
opportunities.why_not_DIY: A chatbot subscription only answers questions typed into its own widget, whereas the actual work is multi-system and stateful: web-form entries, a shared mailbox, a hosted client portal and (likely) a practice-management or calendar tool that do not talk to each other, plus per-office routing rules and an exception queue. It also has to hold an audit trail of who asked for which document and when — the thing an IRS or FTC review would ask for — and it must not leak return information to an unvetted third party. That combination of integration, approval gating, logging and data-handling is engineering, not a subscription.

impact_estimate.range: $4,000–$13,000 per year of recovered staff time (roughly 150–260 hours), plus an unquantified reduction in prospects lost to slow first response
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference, not firm data: 2–3 people touch inbound contact across the two offices; 20–40 inquiries per week in filing season and 5–10 off-season; 6–10 minutes of manual triage, location/service routing and document chasing per inquiry; the agent removes 50–60% of that handling but generates some review work. Valued at the New York–Newark–Jersey City bookkeeping-clerk median of $60,640 (about $29/hour) where administrative staff handle intake, rising to the metro accountant median of $105,650 (about $51/hour) where a CPA does. No client count, call volume or headcount is published, so the range is deliberately wide and the high end assumes the work is being done by billable CPA time.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2–3 weeks, deliberately finished before the January filing season: connect the shared mailbox and the WPForms entries into one queue; ship an intent classifier that routes by office (East Brunswick vs Hazlet) and service line; deploy the per-engagement document checklist with automatic re-request timers; run it in shadow mode for the first week so staff compare its triage to their own; deliver a one-page daily priority digest and a partner approval screen for anything out of policy. Success measure: percentage of inbound items triaged correctly without human correction, and median first-response time versus a pre-pilot baseline the firm supplies.

opportunities.title: HOA/association knowledge and board-package agent (governing docs, budgets, owner Q&A)
opportunities.problem: HOA accounting is one of the firm's nine advertised lines and is unusually document- and question-heavy for a small practice: audits, compliance and reviews, tax prep, forensic accounting, transition to unit-owner control, and budgeting/cash-flow planning for New Jersey associations. Each association brings recurring monthly reporting plus a stream of board and unit-owner questions that can only be answered by digging into that association's own governing documents, prior financials and budgets — repetitive, deadline-driven work that scales linearly with each association added. Meanwhile the firm's HOA page still carries uncustomised 'Who Do We Help?' boilerplate and no HOA-specific content, so there is no self-service layer at all.
evidence: HOA accounting is a listed service line covering audits, compliance, reviews, tax preparation, forensic accounting, unit-owner transitions and budgeting/cash-flow planning for New Jersey associations (https://matthewsandnulty.com/services/hoa-accounting)

The firm advertises nine service lines across two offices, so the same small group of people services associations alongside business tax, payroll and individual returns that all peak in the same quarter (https://matthewsandnulty.com/services/)

HOA pages reuse generic boilerplate aimed at small business / single-member LLC / S-Corp clients rather than association boards, indicating no reusable association-specific answer library exists to hand staff or owners (https://matthewsandnulty.com/services/hoa-accounting)

Field evidence from 79 small and mid-sized firms using an AI accounting platform — a working paper, not peer-reviewed — reports about 8.5% of accountant time reallocated away from routine entry work and a 7.5-day reduction in monthly close time, which is the closest analogue to recurring monthly association reporting (https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/working-papers/human-ai-accounting-early-evidence-field)

Vendor case study (self-reported, no control group) reports 40–50% efficiency on subsequent drafts of financial-statement reviews, used here only as an upper bound (https://www.caseware.com/resources/success-stories/hlb-mann-judd-perth)
opportunities.agent_design: A retrieval agent indexed per association: governing documents and bylaws, management agreements, current and prior budgets, monthly financials, reserve and cash-flow plans, board minutes and the firm's own HOA checklists. Two front ends on the same index. (1) Internal: when an association's month closes, the agent assembles the board package draft — variance commentary against budget, reserve movement, a list of items needing board action — and routes it to the assigned accountant, who reviews and signs. (2) External: a board/owner question channel that answers only from that association's documents, always cites the document and page, refuses and escalates anything about individual unit-owner balances, litigation, or collections, and logs every answer for the file. Triggers: monthly close event, new document upload to the association folder, incoming board or owner email. A licensed professional approves every package and every non-routine answer before it leaves the firm; the agent never posts entries or files anything itself. Deployment is private/on-prem or in a contracted environment with deletion terms, because association financials and owner data sit under the same 7216 and FTC Safeguards Rule constraints as return data (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/7216).
opportunities.why_not_DIY: Generic chatbots have no access to per-association governing documents, cannot keep associations' data separated, and will confidently answer an owner question using the wrong association's bylaws. The value is in permissioned, per-client retrieval over messy PDFs and spreadsheets, mandatory citations for a documented review trail, hard refusal rules on sensitive owner matters, and integration with the monthly close workflow. That is a retrieval and access-control build with a real review gate, which is where the liability lives.

impact_estimate.range: $5,000–$18,000 per year of professional time (roughly 110–350 hours), plus capacity to absorb additional associations without a hire
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference, not firm data: 5–15 associations serviced across the two offices; 4–8 hours per association per month currently spent assembling the board package and answering board/owner questions; the agent removes 30–40% of that (deliberately below the 40–50% vendor-reported figure and below the working paper's close-time effect, because review of the draft still consumes professional time). Valued at the metro accountant median of $105,650 (about $51/hour) since this is CPA/accountant work, not clerical. Association count is not disclosed anywhere, so the low end assumes 5 associations and a 30% saving.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 3–4 weeks on one or two volunteer associations: ingest that association's governing documents, two years of financials and the current budget; build the cited Q&A channel for board members behind a login; generate one board-package draft that the assigned accountant reviews against the version they produced manually, and record the diff. Deliver an escalation policy (what the agent must never answer), a per-association access model, and a written data-handling note covering retention and deletion for the firm's file. Success measure: reviewer-rated accuracy of cited answers on a 20-question test set, and hours per association-month before vs after.

opportunities.title: Payroll run and multi-jurisdiction filing exception agent for the payroll service line
opportunities.problem: Payroll is sold as a full service — state and federal payroll tax filings, paying payroll tax liabilities, direct deposit, a 'dedicated payroll specialist', plus union/certified payroll and workers' comp reporting. That is a monthly-or-more-frequent cycle of small, accuracy-critical, deadline-bound steps (change intake, variance check, filing prep, liability payment, certified-payroll reporting) where one missed jurisdiction or a stale rate produces penalties and amended filings. The firm has no visible automation layer for it — the practice runs on one shared inbox and a generic client portal — and it is being delivered by a small team that is simultaneously selling and filing tax returns in the same window.
evidence: Payroll services advertised include state and federal payroll tax filings, paying payroll tax liabilities, direct deposit, a dedicated payroll specialist, and union/certified payroll and workers' comp reporting — i.e. recurring multi-jurisdiction filing obligations, not a one-off onboarding task (https://matthewsandnulty.com/services/payroll)

O*NET lists 'prepare and process payroll information; calculate and prepare checks for utilities, taxes and other payments' among core bookkeeping-clerk tasks, and 'check figures, postings and documents for correct entry, mathematical accuracy and proper codes' as a central duty — the variance-checking work this agent would pre-stage (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/43-3031.00)

Payroll deadlines collide with the firm's other peak work: individual returns, business returns, payroll filings and association reporting all land in the same January–April window, and O*NET records that 55% of tax preparers work seasonal schedules and 38% face daily time pressure (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/13-2082.00)

Peer-reviewed large-firm evidence (36 largest U.S. audit firms, 2010–2019) found AI-adopting firms cut accounting headcount 3.6% after three years and 7.1% after four, with junior staff down 5.7% and 11.8% — directionally consistent with this work being absorbable by tooling, though the study is about audit at large firms and should not be transferred as an effect size (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11142-022-09697-x)

The FTC Safeguards Rule treats tax preparation firms as financial institutions with encryption, MFA, service-provider oversight and 30-day breach-notification duties, and 26 U.S.C. 7216 makes reckless disclosure of return information a misdemeanour — payroll files carry SSNs, so this work has to run in a contracted or private environment (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/7216)
opportunities.agent_design: A cycle-driven agent per payroll client. It opens when a client's payroll change request arrives (email or portal) or on the scheduled run date, then: parses the request into structured changes (new hire, rate change, hours, deduction), validates each change against the client's prior run, headcount and any union/certified-payroll rules on file, computes the filing calendar for every jurisdiction the client is registered in, drafts the filing set and the liability-payment instructions, and flags anomalies — a 40% swing in gross, a missing timesheet, a new work state, a rate that has not been updated. Triggers: run date, change request, filing due-date countdown (T-5, T-2, T-0), and a liability payment confirmation that never arrived. The 'dedicated payroll specialist' approves every filing and every payment before submission, works a single exception queue, and the agent writes a per-client run log that can be produced on request. It never initiates a payment or transmits a filing on its own.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: Off-the-shelf payroll software already computes taxes, but it does not police the gaps around it: change requests arriving as free-text email, clients registered in jurisdictions the software was never configured for, timesheets that never showed up, liability payments that failed, and certified-payroll rules that differ per job. Closing those gaps means reading unstructured inbound messages, cross-checking against multiple systems and prior periods, driving a deadline calendar, and escalating — with a log an examiner can follow. Reliability and liability, not conversation quality, are the product here, and a chatbot subscription supplies neither.

impact_estimate.range: $4,000–$10,000 per year of payroll-specialist time (roughly 120–320 hours), plus a reduction in late-filing penalties and amended returns that is not quantified here
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference, not firm data: 15–40 payroll clients at 2–4 runs per month; 10–15 minutes per client-run currently spent on change review, variance checking and filing prep; the agent removes 60–75% of that hands-on time but adds exception review. Valued at the New Jersey payroll and timekeeping clerk median of $60,750 (about $30/hour) because a dedicated payroll specialist does this work. Payroll client count and run frequency are not disclosed, so the low end assumes 15 clients at 3 runs/month; penalty savings are excluded from the range rather than estimated.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 3–4 weeks, one payroll client plus a read-only run of three more: build the change-request parser and the variance rules, generate the jurisdiction filing calendar from the firm's own registration list, and produce a daily exception queue with drafted client chase emails. Run entirely in shadow mode against the specialist's real runs, scoring every discrepancy the agent catches or misses — no filings and no payments generated in the pilot. Deliver the exception taxonomy, a per-client run-log format, and a written data-handling and vendor-oversight note that satisfies the firm's Safeguards Rule obligations. Success measure: recall of missed-change and missed-jurisdiction cases on the shadow runs, and specialist minutes per run before vs after.

lead_score.rationale: Sub-scores: pain 18/30, fit 18/20, ability to pay 12/20, ease 12/15, strategic 14/15. Pain (18/30): the structural evidence is solid and sourced — two offices on one phone number and one generic inbox since the late-2023 Hazlet acquisition, a contact form instead of booking, no published hours or after-hours channel, 2022-era marketing and a newsletter form with no submit handler — but it is footprint evidence, not voiced pain. Public reviews are uniformly positive on responsiveness, no complaint about missed calls or slow replies was found, and the firm publishes no client count, headcount or call volume, so the leading opportunity rests on inference from architecture rather than on a client saying 'we lose leads'. Fit (18/20): all three proposals sit squarely in A and C, the client already runs a portal that an agent can read, and the regulatory picture (7216, Safeguards Rule) maps directly onto our private-deployment capability rather than blocking it. Ability to pay (12/20): a likely sub-10-person firm with two named partners, no disclosed revenue or fees, and a Mon–Fri 9–5 footprint — but it just absorbed a second practice, advertises nine service lines including virtual CFO and HOA, and competes in a county with 346 accounting establishments and $149,231 average annual pay, so there is margin and evident appetite to invest in growth. Ease (12/15): one short decision chain (Mike Nulty, with James Matthews), a crisp pilot boundary at the shared inbox, and a natural November–December window before the filing season — discounted because the firm is effectively unreachable by any channel other than phone and form, and a Jan–Apr pilot would die. Strategic (14/15): this is the archetypal New Jersey small CPA practice — 4,396 establishments and 42,391 employees in NAICS 5412 statewide, with accounting graduates down 6.6% year over year and CPA exam candidates falling from 42,626 to 28,082 — so the intake-plus-knowledge-agent pattern built here is resellable to hundreds of similar two-to-three-partner firms. Total 74/100: a strong target whose score is capped mainly by the absence of any first-party statement of pain or of firm size, which the first discovery call should close.

best_evidence_signal: Two offices (East Brunswick plus the Hazlet practice absorbed in late 2023) still run off one shared phone number and one generic inbox with no online booking — the 'Schedule Consultation' button just re-opens a contact form — so inbound work cannot be routed, triaged or measured: https://matthewsandnulty.com/contact
